correctness.rationale: Substitution in the original identity gives B(Px,Py)u = B(x,(P†+P+λI)y)P(u). If P(u)=cu with c nonzero, completing the square gives (P−cI)†(P−cI)=c(c+λ)I, and applying it to u forces c=−λ. The c=0 case is precisely the first family. If u and P(u) are independent, both scalar forms vanish, giving the two adjoint-complementary equations. Conversely each family satisfies the substituted identity (the third does so irrespective of P(u)). In dimension three an isotropic image has rank at most one. A skew-adjoint square-zero map has even rank, so the third family adds only the already-counted zero map at weight zero. At nonzero weight, −P/λ would be an idempotent with two complementary isotropic spaces, impossible in dimension three. The remaining two families are translates and disjoint at nonzero weight since their values on u differ. After finding an isotropic vector by the intersecting two square-value sets, the hyperbolic plane decomposition gives exactly q+1 isotropic lines. Each contributes q²−1 nonzero maps from V/Ku; for square-zero it contributes q−1 unless it is Ku itself, in which case all q²−1 contribute. Adding zero yields all four displayed counts over any odd finite field. A new direct enumeration of all 3⁹ matrices with B=I over F3 and u=(1,0,0) or (1,1,1) confirmed 33, 66, 66 for weights 0,1,2 and the weight-zero square-zero counts 9 and 15. The frozen checker was inspected, not executed. Its j≥i loop is sufficient by symmetry, although its verification note calls the pairs ordered. The finite checks are corroboration, not the proof.
